title: Commercial Interior Design: Balancing Function and Looks
metaTitle: Commercial Interior Design: Function and Looks | Bridgeland
metaDescription: Plan a commercial interior that works first and looks right: code-driven layout choices, durable finishes, lighting, brand colour and flexible design.
excerpt: A practical order of decisions for a commercial interior that works for staff and customers and still looks like your brand, with what to settle early and what can wait.
answer: Decide how the space has to work first, then make it look like your brand within those limits. Settle exits, accessible routes, washrooms, plumbing, ventilation and lighting before choosing finishes, because they are costly to move later. Then pick durable materials, a consistent colour palette and signage that helps customers find their way.

faqs.q: What matters more in a commercial space, function or looks?
faqs.a: Function comes first, because exits, accessibility, plumbing, ventilation and lighting are set by code and are expensive to move. Looks still matter: they shape first impressions and how staff feel at work. The practical answer is to lock in the functional layout, then spend the design budget on the finishes customers see and touch most.

faqs.q: How do I choose colours for my business space?
faqs.a: Start from your brand colours and limit the palette to two or three, plus neutrals. Test samples on site under the lighting you will actually use, since warm and cool LED lighting can change how a colour reads. Use the strongest colour where it does the most work, such as the entrance or a feature wall.

faqs.q: How can I make a small commercial space feel bigger?
faqs.a: Keep sightlines open from the entrance, use lighter colours and the same flooring through connected areas, and light the walls as well as the floor. Glass partitions let light reach interior rooms, and built-in storage keeps clutter off the floor. Make sure any layout change still keeps exits and accessible routes clear.

faqs.q: Are there rules for finishes in a restaurant kitchen?
faqs.a: Yes. Manitoba's guideline for food handling establishments calls for smooth, impervious floors coved and sealed 10 cm up the wall in food preparation and dishwashing areas, smooth, washable, non-absorbent walls and ceilings, and shielded lighting with at least 215 lux on work surfaces. Your public health inspector reviews the plans before construction starts.

faqs.q: Do signs need City approval in Winnipeg?
faqs.a: The City handles sign approvals separately from the building permit, and illuminated signs also need an electrical sign permit taken out by a licensed contractor. Check the City's sign requirements before you order a storefront sign, and plan the wall blocking and power for it before the drywall goes up.

blocks.x: A good commercial interior earns its keep twice: once in how smoothly staff and customers move through it, and again in how clearly it says who you are. When the two clash, function should usually win, because a space that slows service or fails an inspection costs money every day.
This guide sets out an order of decisions that keeps both in view, whether you run a shop, an office, a restaurant or a clinic in Winnipeg.
Why should function come before finishes?

Because the functional parts of a commercial space are the expensive parts to change. Walls that form exits, plumbing for washrooms and sinks, ductwork and electrical are set by code, permits and the building, while paint, décor and loose furniture can change later at modest cost. Fix the first group early and the second group has room to move.

blocks.x: How do Manitoba's accessibility rules shape a commercial layout?

They set minimums for entrances, routes and washrooms. Since January 1, 2024, Manitoba has enforced a building code based on the 2020 National Building Code, which substantially updated accessibility requirements and aligned them with the CSA B651 standard. How they apply to your alteration is settled in plan review, so design for them from the start.

Manitoba also kept three amendments of its own: wider use of visual signal devices, handrails on both sides of stairs and ramps, and rules on how some requirements apply to existing buildings. Design guides written for the United States cite American law that does not apply here; in Manitoba, work from the Manitoba Building Code.

Accessibility does not stop at the drawings. Under Manitoba's Accessible Customer Service Standard, every organization with at least one employee must let the public know when and why an accessibility feature is unavailable, including during a renovation. A separate standard for outdoor public spaces, such as sidewalks and parks, is still in development.
Which finishes hold up in busy commercial spaces?

Commercial-grade finishes chosen for the traffic and cleaning each area gets. Entrances take grit and winter salt, washrooms and kitchens need surfaces that can be scrubbed, and counters and door hardware take constant contact. Spend on durability where wear is heaviest, and save in areas customers rarely see, such as back offices and storage rooms.

blocks.x: Food premises have the most specific rules: Manitoba's guideline calls for smooth, impervious floors in food preparation and dishwashing areas, coved and sealed 10 cm (4 inches) up the wall, and washable, non-absorbent walls and ceilings. Our guide to [restaurant renovation permits in Winnipeg](/blog/restaurant-renovation-permits-winnipeg) covers the rest.
How much does lighting change a commercial space?

More than most owners expect. Lighting decides whether staff can work comfortably, whether products and food look right, and whether the room feels calm or harsh. Plan general lighting for safety and cleaning, task lighting where work happens, and accent lighting for displays or brand features, then choose fixture styles to suit.

Some spaces have minimum levels: Manitoba's food premises guideline requires at least 215 lux (20 foot-candles) on food preparation and dishwashing work surfaces, with shielded fixtures. If you are replacing lighting, Efficiency Manitoba runs a Business Lighting Program; apply first, because it says not to buy materials or start the project until your application is approved.
How do you carry a brand through a space without overspending?

Choose a small palette and repeat it. Two or three brand colours, one or two signature materials and a consistent signage style, used at the entrance, the main counter and one feature wall, do more than scattering branded details everywhere. Standard materials elsewhere keep the budget for the places customers actually look.
**Colour:** test paint and laminate samples under your actual lighting before you commit.
**Materials:** give customers one surface to touch that carries the brand, such as a wood counter edge or a tiled service front.
**Flow:** a clear path from the door to the counter or reception tells people where to go before any sign does.
**Signage:** plan sign locations, power and wall blocking before drywall. The City handles signs separately, and illuminated signs need an electrical sign permit.
**Lease length:** attached improvements usually stay with the building, so on a short lease put more of the brand into furniture and fixtures you can take with you.
How do you keep a commercial layout flexible?

Build in what will not change and keep the rest movable. Fixed walls, plumbing and ventilation should follow the long-term plan, while workstations, displays and seating should be furniture you can rearrange. Extra power and data capacity, and lighting that does not depend on today's furniture layout, make later changes cheaper.
